Our article Why do singers wear in-ear monitors on stage? drew plenty of attention and discussion. In-ear monitors are in fact a kind of monitor headphone, so this article looks at monitor headphones in general. Monitor headphones are designed for audio production and professional monitoring, and their defining feature is that they reproduce the original sound as faithfully as possible. As the name suggests, “monitoring” means listening to the audio signal in real time without cosmetically enhancing or coloring it. Monitor headphones therefore let you hear something close to the original source, with a wide frequency response and very low distortion. In principle they work just like ordinary dynamic headphones, but their tuning emphasizes a flat frequency response and low distortion, so that every note is reproduced clearly, without favoring any frequency range.

How they differ from consumer headphones

Sound: monitor headphones aim to reproduce the original sound with almost no tonal coloring, giving very high fidelity, whereas ordinary consumer headphones often boost the bass or treble to enrich the sound and make music more “pleasing.” The same source therefore sounds more neutral and flat on monitor headphones, while on ordinary headphones it often has more “atmosphere” but also more distortion.

Where they are used: monitor headphones are mainly used in professional settings such as recording studios, broadcast studios and live performance, where the sound has to be captured and adjusted precisely; ordinary headphones are made for entertainment, such as listening to music, watching films and gaming.

Build and comfort: monitor headphones usually have a closed-back design with large earcups to block out ambient noise. They are sturdy and durable but generally heavier and clamp more firmly, so over long sessions they may feel less light than ordinary headphones. Ordinary headphones put more weight on lightness and comfort: they are smaller, clamp less tightly, travel more easily and suit long wear better.

Typical uses

Monitor headphones are everywhere in professional audio work, including but not limited to:

Recording: when tracking singers or instruments in the studio, the recording engineer uses monitor headphones to listen to the incoming signal in real time, catch noise or mistakes and correct them promptly.

Mixing and mastering: mix engineers use monitor headphones to balance the instruments and fine-tune frequencies and effects, so as to arrive at a well-balanced final mix.

Broadcasting and podcasting: in radio stations, podcast recordings and live streams, hosts and sound engineers use monitor headphones to check the microphones and the audio output, keeping level, speech intelligibility and sound quality stable.

Live performance and DJing: singers, musicians and DJs wear monitor headphones on stage, both to shut out stage noise and to hear their own voice or the backing track precisely, so they stay in tune and on the beat.

Other professional settings: film post-production, simultaneous interpreting, conference monitoring and other fields that call for accurate listening also rely on monitor headphones.

Are they good for everyday listening?

For everyday listening, monitor headphones behave differently from ordinary headphones. Their strength is a truthful, unembellished sound with clear detail, which lets demanding listeners hear tiny differences in the original recording. But that is also their weakness: without boosted bass or treble to “beautify” the sound, they can sound flat, even so clean as to seem a little “thin,” and some pop music may lack bass weight or emotional color on them. Monitor headphones are also built to be sturdy, with a firm clamping force, and over long periods they may be less comfortable than dedicated hi-fi headphones. In short, if you want to hear music as close as possible to the original, monitor headphones will reveal more detail; if you just want to relax or enjoy music with impact, ordinary headphones are often more enjoyable.

Buying advice

Closed-back vs. open-back: monitor headphones come in closed-back and open-back designs. Closed-back headphones have a sealed rear chamber; they isolate well and suit recording or noisy environments, but can sound a little boxed in. Closed designs can be further divided into over-ear and in-ear types, and the in-ear type is the in-ear monitor. Open-back headphones have a vented rear chamber; they sound more natural and open, with a wide soundstage and less fatigue over long sessions, but they do not isolate and they leak sound. For quiet use at home, either works, depending on taste; if you need to take them out or record with them, closed-back is generally the safer choice.

Comfort: monitor headphones are often worn for long working sessions, so their headbands and earpads usually use memory foam and other ergonomic materials and are fairly comfortable. Try them on or read reviews before buying, paying attention to earcup size, clamping force and overall weight, and avoid earpads that are too hard or a clamp so tight that it causes soreness. In general, somewhat pricier professional monitors do better on comfort.

Impedance and connections: some monitor headphones have a high impedance and need a professional audio interface or headphone amplifier to drive them properly; an ordinary source may not have enough power. For everyday use, an impedance of roughly 32–80 Ω keeps them compatible with phones, computers and similar devices.

Brands and models: the well-known manufacturers all have classic monitor models, such as the Sony MDR-7506 (closed-back, affordable, excellent isolation, comfortable), the Sennheiser HD 280 Pro (closed-back, good isolation, durable and great value) and the Audio-Technica ATH-M50x (closed-back, with well-resolved bass). Beyerdynamic’s DT series, Shure’s SRH series and the AKG K240 (semi-open) are also common monitor headphones in music production. Pick a tier that fits your budget and needs, weighing the points above.

In short, monitor headphones are built for professional monitoring. If accuracy matters a great deal to you, or you need them for recording and production, they are a good choice; if you just want comfortable everyday listening, a good pair of ordinary hi-fi headphones may suit you better.
